subtopics.title: T6 Rates and Equilibrium · AQA Chemistry

questions.question:
A reaction produces 72 cm3 of gas in 90 s.
The tangent to the curve at 20 s passes through (10 s, 18 cm3) and (40 s, 57 cm3).
Part (a): Calculate the mean rate.
Part (b): Give the unit.
Part (c): Calculate the instantaneous rate at 20 s.
questions.modelAnswer:
Mean = 72/90 = 0.80 cm3/s.
Instantaneous rate = gradient = (57-18)/(40-10) = 1.30 cm3/s.
Use points on the tangent, not the curve.
markingPoints: Instantaneous rate = gradient = (57-18)/(40-10) = 1.30 cm3/s.
Use points on the tangent, not the curve.

questions.question:
Two gas-volume curves reach 60 cm3.
Curve A reaches the plateau in 40 s and B in 85 s.
State what can and cannot be concluded about rate, limiting amount and possible conditions.
questions.modelAnswer:
A has greater initial/mean rate.
Equal plateaux show equal final gas amount and likely same moles of limiting reactant.
Difference could be temperature, concentration, pressure, surface area or catalyst.
Curve alone cannot identify which.
markingPoints: A has greater initial/mean rate.
Equal plateaux show equal final gas amount and likely same moles of limiting reactant.
Difference could be temperature, concentration, pressure, surface area or catalyst.
Curve alone cannot identify which.

questions.question:
A solid loses 1.84 g in 230 s.
The balance reads to 0.01 g and time to 1 s.
Part (a): Calculate mean mass-loss rate.
Part (b): Explain which change would reduce percentage uncertainty in the mass change.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Rate = 1.84/230 = 0.0080 g/s.
(b) Measure a larger mass change/use balance with finer resolution.
Larger measured change makes fixed absolute uncertainty a smaller percentage.
Repeats do not remove systematic error.
markingPoints: (b) Measure a larger mass change/use balance with finer resolution.
Larger measured change makes fixed absolute uncertainty a smaller percentage.
Repeats do not remove systematic error.

questions.question: A reaction time falls from 120 s to 48 s for the same fixed change. Calculate the rate-factor increase using 1/time.
questions.modelAnswer:
Factor = (1/48)/(1/120) = 120/48 = 2.5
Rate is 2.5 times greater.
markingPoints: Rate is 2.5 times greater.

questions.question: Identify the limiting evidence needed before claiming that a changed condition altered yield rather than only rate in a gas-producing experiment.
questions.modelAnswer:
Need complete curves/plateau values.
Same starting moles and limiting reactant.
Airtight apparatus/same conditions.
Compare final gas amount after reaction completion, not volume at a fixed early time.
markingPoints: Need complete curves/plateau values.
Same starting moles and limiting reactant.
Airtight apparatus/same conditions.
Compare final gas amount after reaction completion, not volume at a fixed early time.

questions.question: State two ways the rate of a reaction can be measured.
questions.modelAnswer:
Measure the quantity of reactant used or product formed per unit time.
Examples include gas volume, mass loss, concentration or precipitate formation.
markingPoints: Measure the quantity of reactant used or product formed per unit time.
Examples include gas volume, mass loss, concentration or precipitate formation.

questions.question: Write the equation used to calculate the mean rate of a reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: Mean rate = quantity of reactant used or quantity of product formed divided by time.
markingPoints: Mean rate = quantity of reactant used or quantity of product formed divided by time.

questions.question: The concentration of a reactant falls from 0.80 mol/dm3 to 0.32 mol/dm3 in 40 s. Calculate the mean rate at which it is used.
questions.modelAnswer:
Change = 0.48 mol/dm3.
Rate = 0.48/40 = 0.012 mol/dm3/s.
markingPoints: Change = 0.48 mol/dm3.

questions.question: Why is the gradient of a product–time graph usually steepest near the start of a reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: Reactant concentrations are highest initially, so collisions are most frequent and there are most successful collisions per second.
markingPoints: Reactant concentrations are highest initially, so collisions are most frequent and there are most successful collisions per second.

questions.question: A gas-volume graph reaches 48 cm³ after 80 s. Draw-tangent information gives points (30 s, 20 cm³) and (50 s, 34 cm³). Calculate rate at 40 s.
questions.modelAnswer: Gradient = change in volume ÷ change in time = (34−20) ÷ (50−30) = 14 ÷ 20 = 0.70 cm³/s.
markingPoints: Gradient = change in volume ÷ change in time = (34−20) ÷ (50−30) = 14 ÷ 20 = 0.70 cm³/s.

questions.question: Describe how to determine the initial rate from a product-volume graph.
questions.modelAnswer:
Draw a tangent to the curve at time zero.
Choose two well-separated points on the tangent.
Calculate gradient = change in volume ÷ change in time
Include units.
markingPoints: Draw a tangent to the curve at time zero.
Choose two well-separated points on the tangent.
Calculate gradient = change in volume ÷ change in time
Include units.

questions.question: How do you measure the rate of a chemical reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: By measuring the the quantity of the reactant as it is used or the quantity of the product as it is formed.
markingPoints: By measuring the the quantity of the reactant as it is used or the quantity of the product as it is formed.

questions.question: What is the formula to calculate measure the mean rate of reaction from the reactants?
questions.modelAnswer: Mean rate of reaction = quantity of reactant used / time taken.
markingPoints: Mean rate of reaction = quantity of reactant used / time taken.

questions.question: What is the formula to calculate the mean rate of reaction from the products?
questions.modelAnswer: Mean rate of reaction = quantity of product formed / time taken.
markingPoints: Mean rate of reaction = quantity of product formed / time taken.

questions.question: What three quantities can be used to measure the the quantity of the product or reactant?
questions.modelAnswer: Mass in grams, volume in cm3 or moles.
markingPoints: Mass in grams, volume in cm3 or moles.

questions.question: What are the units for rate of reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: g/s, cm3/s or mol/s
markingPoints: g/s, cm3/s or mol/s

questions.question: What is a tangent?
questions.modelAnswer: A straight line that touches a curve at one point and shows the gradient at that point.
markingPoints: A straight line that touches a curve at one point and shows the gradient at that point.

questions.question: What is the slope of a tangent used to calculate?
questions.modelAnswer: The instantaneous rate of reaction at that point.
markingPoints: The instantaneous rate of reaction at that point.

questions.question: On a concentration–time graph, what does the gradient of a tangent represent?
questions.modelAnswer: The instantaneous rate of reaction at that point.
markingPoints: The instantaneous rate of reaction at that point.

questions.question: Part (a): Explain, using collision theory, why powdered calcium carbonate reacts faster than equal-mass lumps with the same acid, but produces the same final gas volume when acid is in excess.
questions.modelAnswer:
Powder has greater surface area.
More particles are exposed.
Collision frequency and successful collisions per second increase.
Same moles of limiting calcium carbonate produce the same moles/final volume of CO2.
markingPoints: Powder has greater surface area.
More particles are exposed.
Collision frequency and successful collisions per second increase.
Same moles of limiting calcium carbonate produce the same moles/final volume of CO2.

questions.question:
A student investigates concentration using sodium thiosulfate and acid and times how long a cross takes to disappear.
Part (a): Give a valid method, variables, one safety control and two improvements.
questions.modelAnswer:
Measure fixed volumes.
Vary thiosulfate concentration while keeping total volume/acid volume and concentration/temperature/depth constant.
Mix and start timer.
Stop when cross disappears.
Rate proxy 1/time.
Wear eye protection.
Repeat and mean.
Use light sensor/colorimeter or same observer/end point.
Water bath.
Systematic concentration series.
markingPoints: Measure fixed volumes.
Vary thiosulfate concentration while keeping total volume/acid volume and concentration/temperature/depth constant.
Mix and start timer.
Stop when cross disappears.
Rate proxy 1/time.
Wear eye protection.
Repeat and mean.
Use light sensor/colorimeter or same observer/end point.
Water bath.
Systematic concentration series.

questions.question: Explain why doubling concentration does not always exactly double measured rate in a school experiment.
questions.modelAnswer:
Collision frequency expected to rise, but relationship may not be directly proportional.
Temperature may change.
Mixing/timing/end-point limitations.
Gas leakage.
Concentration uncertainty.
Other reactant or surface becomes controlling.
markingPoints: Collision frequency expected to rise, but relationship may not be directly proportional.
Temperature may change.
Mixing/timing/end-point limitations.
Gas leakage.
Concentration uncertainty.
Other reactant or surface becomes controlling.

questions.question: Explain why increasing the concentration of a solution increases reaction rate.
questions.modelAnswer: There are more reactant particles per unit volume, collisions occur more frequently, and so there are more successful collisions per second.
markingPoints: There are more reactant particles per unit volume, collisions occur more frequently, and so there are more successful collisions per second.

questions.question: Explain why increasing the pressure of reacting gases increases reaction rate.
questions.modelAnswer: Gas particles are closer together/more particles occupy each unit volume, so collision frequency and successful collisions per second increase.
markingPoints: Gas particles are closer together/more particles occupy each unit volume, so collision frequency and successful collisions per second increase.

questions.question: Explain two systematic errors in a gas-syringe rate experiment and how each affects results.
questions.modelAnswer:
Gas escaping before stopper insertion makes recorded volumes/rate too low.
Leaking apparatus also lowers volume.
A sticking plunger can delay/under-record volume.
Fit stopper promptly, test seals and ensure syringe moves freely.
markingPoints: Gas escaping before stopper insertion makes recorded volumes/rate too low.
Leaking apparatus also lowers volume.
A sticking plunger can delay/under-record volume.
Fit stopper promptly, test seals and ensure syringe moves freely.

questions.question: Plan an investigation of the effect of hydrochloric acid concentration on the rate of reaction with marble chips using a gas syringe.
questions.modelAnswer:
Use equal masses and surface areas of marble.
Use equal acid volumes at several concentrations.
Connect rapidly to a gas syringe.
Record gas volume at regular times.
Keep temperature constant.
Repeat.
Calculate initial rate from the early gradient.
markingPoints: Use equal masses and surface areas of marble.
Use equal acid volumes at several concentrations.
Connect rapidly to a gas syringe.
Record gas volume at regular times.
Keep temperature constant.
Repeat.
Calculate initial rate from the early gradient.

questions.question: Explain why inserting the bung slowly causes a systematic error in a gas-volume rate experiment.
questions.modelAnswer:
The reaction begins before sealing, so gas escapes unmeasured.
Volumes are consistently too low, especially early readings.
Practise or use apparatus that can be sealed before mixing.
markingPoints: The reaction begins before sealing, so gas escapes unmeasured.
Volumes are consistently too low, especially early readings.
Practise or use apparatus that can be sealed before mixing.

questions.question: Compare the strengths and limitations of mass-loss and gas-syringe methods for measuring reaction rate.
questions.modelAnswer:
Mass loss gives continuous objective readings but only works when gas escapes and can be affected by evaporation/draughts.
A gas syringe directly measures gas volume but may leak, stick or have limited capacity.
Choice depends on reaction and required resolution.
markingPoints: Mass loss gives continuous objective readings but only works when gas escapes and can be affected by evaporation/draughts.
A gas syringe directly measures gas volume but may leak, stick or have limited capacity.
Choice depends on reaction and required resolution.

questions.question: Name five factors which affect the rate of chemical reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: Concentration of reactants, pressure of reacting gases, surface area of reactants, temperature of the reaction and the presence of catalysts.
markingPoints: Concentration of reactants, pressure of reacting gases, surface area of reactants, temperature of the reaction and the presence of catalysts.

questions.question: Describe the effect of changing these factors on the rate of chemical reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: Increasing concentration of reactants increases the number of colliding molecules. Increasing pressure of reacting gases increases the number of collisions between molecules. Large surface area of reactants increases number of colliding molecules. Increasing temperature of the reaction increases number of collisions. The presence of catalysts lowers the activation energy.
markingPoints: Increasing concentration of reactants increases the number of colliding molecules. Increasing pressure of reacting gases increases the number of collisions between molecules. Large surface area of reactants increases number of colliding molecules. Increasing temperature of the reaction increases number of collisions. The presence of catalysts lowers the activation energy.

questions.question: What is turbidity?
questions.modelAnswer: A measure of how cloudy a solution is.
markingPoints: A measure of how cloudy a solution is.

questions.question: Describe an experiment involving colour change or turbidity to measure the effect of concentration on the rate of reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: Add a set volume and concentration of sodium thiosulfate to a conical flask. Place the flask on a black cross drawn on paper. Add a known volume of hydrochloric acid to the conical flask. Start the stopwatch. Time how long it takes for the cross to disappear (due to turbidity of the reacting solution). Repeat the reaction for different concentrations of hydrochloric acid.
markingPoints: Add a set volume and concentration of sodium thiosulfate to a conical flask. Place the flask on a black cross drawn on paper. Add a known volume of hydrochloric acid to the conical flask. Start the stopwatch. Time how long it takes for the cross to disappear (due to turbidity of the reacting solution). Repeat the reaction for different concentrations of hydrochloric acid.

questions.question: Describe an experiment involving the collection of gas to measure the effect of concentration on the rate of reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: Add a set volume and concentration of hydrochloric acid to a conical flask. Add a set mass of magnesium to the flask. Place a bung with a tube attached to a gas syringe on top of the flask. Start the timer. Note the volume of gas produced every 20 seconds until the reaction stops. Repeat the experiment using different concentrations of hydrochloric acid.
markingPoints: Add a set volume and concentration of hydrochloric acid to a conical flask. Add a set mass of magnesium to the flask. Place a bung with a tube attached to a gas syringe on top of the flask. Start the timer. Note the volume of gas produced every 20 seconds until the reaction stops. Repeat the experiment using different concentrations of hydrochloric acid.

questions.question: Explain fully why increasing temperature increases reaction rate. Include both changes to particle behaviour required for full marks.
questions.modelAnswer:
Particles move faster, so collide more frequently.
Collisions have greater energies.
A larger fraction have energy at least equal to activation energy.
More successful collisions per second.
markingPoints: Particles move faster, so collide more frequently.
Collisions have greater energies.
A larger fraction have energy at least equal to activation energy.
More successful collisions per second.

questions.question: Define activation energy.
questions.modelAnswer: The minimum energy particles must have when they collide for a reaction to occur.
markingPoints: The minimum energy particles must have when they collide for a reaction to occur.

questions.question: Explain collision theory?
questions.modelAnswer: Chemical reactions occur when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy.
markingPoints: Chemical reactions occur when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy.

questions.question: Describe the effect of increasing the concentration of reactants on the reaction rate using collision theory?
questions.modelAnswer: Higher concentration means more particles in a given volume, so collisions happen more frequently and the rate increases.
markingPoints: Higher concentration means more particles in a given volume, so collisions happen more frequently and the rate increases.

questions.question: Describe the effect of increasing the pressure of reactants on the reaction rate using collision theory?
questions.modelAnswer: Higher pressure means more gas particles in a given volume, so collisions happen more frequently and the rate increases.
markingPoints: Higher pressure means more gas particles in a given volume, so collisions happen more frequently and the rate increases.

questions.question: Describe the effect of increasing the surface area of reactants on the reaction rate using collision theory?
questions.modelAnswer: Greater surface area exposes more particles, so collisions happen more frequently and the rate increases.
markingPoints: Greater surface area exposes more particles, so collisions happen more frequently and the rate increases.

questions.question: How does the surface area to volume ratio affect the rate of reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: Breaking up a solid into smaller pieces increases the surface area to volume ratio which will speed up the rate of reaction.
markingPoints: Breaking up a solid into smaller pieces increases the surface area to volume ratio which will speed up the rate of reaction.

questions.question: Describe the effect of increasing the temperature of reactants on the reaction rate using collision theory?
questions.modelAnswer: Higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy. They move faster, collide more often and a greater proportion have energy above the activation energy.
markingPoints: Higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy. They move faster, collide more often and a greater proportion have energy above the activation energy.

questions.question:
Design an investigation of catalyst concentration on hydrogen peroxide decomposition using a gas syringe.
Part (a): State how to obtain initial rate and how to decide whether catalyst changes final yield.
questions.modelAnswer:
Fixed H2O2 volume/concentration/temperature.
Vary catalyst amount or concentration.
Airtight gas syringe.
Start together.
Record gas volume at short regular intervals.
Repeats/mean.
Initial rate from initial gradient.
Compare plateau gas volumes.
Catalyst should not alter final yield if starting limiting reagent unchanged.
markingPoints: Fixed H2O2 volume/concentration/temperature.
Vary catalyst amount or concentration.
Airtight gas syringe.
Start together.
Record gas volume at short regular intervals.
Repeats/mean.
Initial rate from initial gradient.
Compare plateau gas volumes.
Catalyst should not alter final yield if starting limiting reagent unchanged.

questions.question: Explain how a catalyst changes a reaction profile and the reaction rate.
questions.modelAnswer: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy. More particles have enough energy for successful collisions, so the reaction rate increases.
markingPoints: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy. More particles have enough energy for successful collisions, so the reaction rate increases.

questions.question: State two things that a catalyst does not change.
questions.modelAnswer: A catalyst does not change the overall energy change of a reaction or the amounts/yield of products at equilibrium.
markingPoints: A catalyst does not change the overall energy change of a reaction or the amounts/yield of products at equilibrium.

questions.question: A catalyst is recovered unchanged after a reaction. Explain why this observation is expected.
questions.modelAnswer: A catalyst increases rate but is not chemically changed or used up overall in the reaction.
markingPoints: A catalyst increases rate but is not chemically changed or used up overall in the reaction.

questions.question: Explain why increasing temperature often changes rate more than a similar increase in concentration.
questions.modelAnswer:
Both increase collision frequency, but higher temperature also shifts the energy distribution so a much larger fraction of particles has energy at least equal to activation energy.
Successful collisions rise substantially.
markingPoints: Both increase collision frequency, but higher temperature also shifts the energy distribution so a much larger fraction of particles has energy at least equal to activation energy.
Successful collisions rise substantially.

questions.question: What is a catalyst?
questions.modelAnswer: A substance that changes the rate of a chemical reaction but is not used up in the process.
markingPoints: A substance that changes the rate of a chemical reaction but is not used up in the process.

questions.question: How do catalysts work?
questions.modelAnswer: Catalysts work by providing a pathway for the reaction which has a lower activation energy.
markingPoints: Catalysts work by providing a pathway for the reaction which has a lower activation energy.

questions.question: What are enzymes?
questions.modelAnswer: Enzymes are biological catalysts found in living organisms.
markingPoints: Enzymes are biological catalysts found in living organisms.

questions.question: What does the symbol ⇌ show in a chemical equation?
questions.modelAnswer: The reaction is reversible: products can react to form the original reactants as well as the forward reaction occurring.
markingPoints: The reaction is reversible: products can react to form the original reactants as well as the forward reaction occurring.

questions.question: What is a reversible reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: A reaction where the products of the reaction can react to produce the original reactants.
markingPoints: A reaction where the products of the reaction can react to produce the original reactants.

questions.question: Represent a reversible reaction with the reactants A and B and the products C and D?
questions.modelAnswer: A + B ⇌ C + D.
markingPoints: A + B ⇌ C + D.

questions.question: How can the direction of a reversible reaction be changed?
questions.modelAnswer: By changing the conditions of the reaction.
markingPoints: By changing the conditions of the reaction.

questions.question: How can the direction of the decomposition of ammonium chloride into ammonia and hydrogen chloride be changed?
questions.modelAnswer: Ammonium chloride ⇌ ammonia + hydrogen chloride. If heated the reaction will move to the right (produce ammonia and hydrogen chloride). If cooled the reaction will move to the left (produce ammonium chloride).
markingPoints: Ammonium chloride ⇌ ammonia + hydrogen chloride. If heated the reaction will move to the right (produce ammonia and hydrogen chloride). If cooled the reaction will move to the left (produce ammonium chloride).

questions.question: Hydrated copper sulfate is heated. State the colour change and name the products.
questions.modelAnswer: Blue hydrated copper sulfate forms white anhydrous copper sulfate and water.
markingPoints: Blue hydrated copper sulfate forms white anhydrous copper sulfate and water.

questions.question: If the forward direction of a reversible reaction transfers 75 kJ to the surroundings, state the energy change of the reverse reaction.
questions.modelAnswer:
The reverse reaction takes in 75 kJ
It has the same magnitude but opposite sign/direction.
markingPoints: The reverse reaction takes in 75 kJ
It has the same magnitude but opposite sign/direction.

questions.question: If a reaction is exothermic in one direction what will it be in the opposite direction?
questions.modelAnswer: Endothermic.
markingPoints: Endothermic.

questions.question: What does hydrated mean?
questions.modelAnswer: The compound is associated with water molecules.
markingPoints: The compound is associated with water molecules.

questions.question: What does anhydrous mean?
questions.modelAnswer: The compound has no water molecules associated with it.
markingPoints: The compound has no water molecules associated with it.

questions.question: What are energy changes associated with the reversible reaction of hydrated copper sulfate changing into anhydrous copper sulfate and water?
questions.modelAnswer: Hydrated copper sulfate ⇌ anhydrous copper sulfate + water. The reaction is endothermic to the right (formation of anhydrous copper sulfate) and exothermic to the right (formation of hydrated copper sulfate).
markingPoints: Hydrated copper sulfate ⇌ anhydrous copper sulfate + water. The reaction is endothermic to the right (formation of anhydrous copper sulfate) and exothermic to the right (formation of hydrated copper sulfate).

questions.question: What is equilibrium?
questions.modelAnswer: Equilibrium occurs when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate (no apparent change).
markingPoints: Equilibrium occurs when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate (no apparent change).

questions.question: What is a closed system?
questions.modelAnswer: Apparatus which prevents the escape of the products or reactants of a reaction.
markingPoints: Apparatus which prevents the escape of the products or reactants of a reaction.

questions.question: Design an experiment to test whether a catalyst changes equilibrium yield as well as time to equilibrium.
questions.modelAnswer:
Run identical closed systems at the same temperature, pressure and starting concentrations, with and without catalyst.
Monitor concentration over time.
Compare time to constant concentrations and final equilibrium concentrations.
Repeat.
Catalyst should shorten time but not change final composition.
markingPoints: Run identical closed systems at the same temperature, pressure and starting concentrations, with and without catalyst.
Monitor concentration over time.
Compare time to constant concentrations and final equilibrium concentrations.
Repeat.
Catalyst should shorten time but not change final composition.

questions.question: What do the relative amounts of reactants and products at equilibrium depend upon?
questions.modelAnswer: They depend on the conditions of the reaction.
markingPoints: They depend on the conditions of the reaction.

questions.question: Describe what happens to a system at equilibrium when a change is made to one of the conditions?
questions.modelAnswer: The system will respond to counteract the change.
markingPoints: The system will respond to counteract the change.

questions.question: What is Le Chatelier’s principle?
questions.modelAnswer: If the conditions of a reaction in equilibrium are changed the system will respond to counteract the change. This results in a new point of equilibrium.
markingPoints: If the conditions of a reaction in equilibrium are changed the system will respond to counteract the change. This results in a new point of equilibrium.

questions.question: Where will the position of equilibrium be when ammonium chloride is heated?
questions.modelAnswer: To the right (ammonia and hydrogen chloride formed).
markingPoints: To the right (ammonia and hydrogen chloride formed).

questions.question: Where will the position of equilibrium be when ammonia and hydrogen chloride are cooled?
questions.modelAnswer: To the left (ammonium chloride formed).
markingPoints: To the left (ammonium chloride formed).

questions.question: Where will the position of equilibrium be when hydrated copper sulfate is heated?
questions.modelAnswer: To the right (anhydrous copper sulfate and water formed).
markingPoints: To the right (anhydrous copper sulfate and water formed).

questions.question: Describe what happens if the concentration of a reactant or product in a reversible reaction is changed?
questions.modelAnswer: The system will no longer be in equilibrium. The concentrations of the substance will change until equilibrium is reached again.
markingPoints: The system will no longer be in equilibrium. The concentrations of the substance will change until equilibrium is reached again.

questions.question: Describe the effect of increasing the concentration of a reactant in a reversible reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: More products will be formed until equilibrium is reached.
markingPoints: More products will be formed until equilibrium is reached.

questions.question: Describe the effect of decreasing the concentration of a product in a reversible reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: More reactants will react until equilibrium is reached.
markingPoints: More reactants will react until equilibrium is reached.

questions.question: What happens is more nitrogen is added in the following reaction: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3?
questions.modelAnswer: More is NH3 produced.
markingPoints: More is NH3 produced.

questions.question: What happens is more hydrogen is added in the following reaction: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3?
questions.modelAnswer: More is NH3 produced.
markingPoints: More is NH3 produced.

questions.question: What happens if the concentration of ammonia is decreased in the following reaction? N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3?
questions.modelAnswer: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3? More N2 + 3H2 will react.
markingPoints: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3? More N2 + 3H2 will react.

questions.question: For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, explain the effects of increasing pressure and adding an iron catalyst.
questions.modelAnswer:
Higher pressure shifts equilibrium right because gas moles fall from 4 to 2, increasing ammonia yield and collision frequency.
Iron lowers activation energy and speeds both directions equally, reaching equilibrium faster without changing yield.
markingPoints: Higher pressure shifts equilibrium right because gas moles fall from 4 to 2, increasing ammonia yield and collision frequency.
Iron lowers activation energy and speeds both directions equally, reaching equilibrium faster without changing yield.

questions.question: Describe the effect of increasing the temperature of a system at equilibrium on the relative amount of products for an exothermic reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: The relative amount of products at equilibrium decrease.
markingPoints: The relative amount of products at equilibrium decrease.

questions.question: Describe the effect of increasing the temperature of a system at equilibrium on the relative amount of products for an endothermic reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: The relative amount of products at equilibrium increase.
markingPoints: The relative amount of products at equilibrium increase.

questions.question: Describe the effect of decreasing the temperature of a system at equilibrium on the relative amount of products for an exothermic reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: The relative amount of products at equilibrium increase.
markingPoints: The relative amount of products at equilibrium increase.

questions.question: Describe the effect of decreasing the temperature of a system at equilibrium on the relative amount of products for an endothermic reaction?
questions.modelAnswer: The relative amount of products at equilibrium decrease.
markingPoints: The relative amount of products at equilibrium decrease.

questions.question: The following reaction is exothermic in the forward direction and endothermic in the opposite direction: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3. Describe what happens if the temperature is decreased?
questions.modelAnswer: The relative amounts of NH3 will increase at equilibrium.
markingPoints: The relative amounts of NH3 will increase at equilibrium.

questions.question: The following reaction is exothermic in the forward direction and endothermic in the opposite direction: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3. Describe what happens if the temperature is increased?
questions.modelAnswer: The relative amounts of NH3 will decrease at equilibrium.
markingPoints: The relative amounts of NH3 will decrease at equilibrium.

questions.question: Describe the effect of decreasing the pressure of a gaseous reaction at equilibrium?
questions.modelAnswer: A decrease in pressure will cause the reaction to shift to the side with the larger number of molecules (from the balanced symbol equation).
markingPoints: A decrease in pressure will cause the reaction to shift to the side with the larger number of molecules (from the balanced symbol equation).

questions.question: Describe the effect of increasing the pressure of a gaseous reaction at equilibrium?
questions.modelAnswer: An increase in pressure will cause the reaction to shift to the side with the smaller number of molecules (from the balanced symbol equation).
markingPoints: An increase in pressure will cause the reaction to shift to the side with the smaller number of molecules (from the balanced symbol equation).

questions.question: Describe what will happen to the equilibrium position if the pressure is increased for the following reaction: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3?
questions.modelAnswer: The are less molecules on the left (2 moles compared to 4 moles) so the reaction will shift to the right (more NH3).
markingPoints: The are less molecules on the left (2 moles compared to 4 moles) so the reaction will shift to the right (more NH3).

questions.question: Describe what will happen to the equilibrium position if the pressure is decreased for the following reaction: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3?
questions.modelAnswer: The are more molecules on the right (4 moles compared to 2 moles) so the reaction will shift to the left (more N2 + H2).
markingPoints: The are more molecules on the right (4 moles compared to 2 moles) so the reaction will shift to the left (more N2 + H2).

questions.question: Define dynamic equilibrium.
questions.modelAnswer: In a closed system, the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate.
markingPoints: In a closed system, the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate.

questions.question: Explain why the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant at dynamic equilibrium.
questions.modelAnswer: The forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so reactants and products are made and used up at equal rates.
markingPoints: The forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so reactants and products are made and used up at equal rates.

questions.question: State the two conditions needed for dynamic equilibrium to be established.
questions.modelAnswer: The reaction must be reversible and occur in a closed system.
markingPoints: The reaction must be reversible and occur in a closed system.

questions.question: Explain why a catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium.
questions.modelAnswer:
It lowers activation energy and speeds both forward and reverse reactions equally.
Equilibrium is reached sooner but equilibrium concentrations/yield are unchanged.

questions.question: Define a closed system in the context of dynamic equilibrium.
questions.modelAnswer: A system in which no substances can enter or leave.
markingPoints: A system in which no substances can enter or leave.

questions.question: For A(aq) ⇌ B(aq), predict the effect of removing B from an equilibrium mixture.
questions.modelAnswer: The equilibrium shifts to the right to replace B, so more B is formed.
markingPoints: The equilibrium shifts to the right to replace B, so more B is formed.

questions.question: For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), the forward reaction is endothermic. Predict and explain the effect of increasing pressure on the yield of NO₂.
questions.modelAnswer: The yield of NO₂ decreases. Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium to the side with fewer gas molecules, which is N₂O₄.
markingPoints: The yield of NO₂ decreases. Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium to the side with fewer gas molecules, which is N₂O₄.

questions.question: For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), the forward reaction is endothermic. Predict and explain the effect of increasing temperature on the yield of NO₂.
questions.modelAnswer: The yield of NO₂ increases. Higher temperature favours the endothermic forward reaction.
markingPoints: The yield of NO₂ increases. Higher temperature favours the endothermic forward reaction.

questions.question: For an exothermic forward reaction, predict the effect of decreasing temperature on product yield.
questions.modelAnswer: The equilibrium shifts in the exothermic forward direction to oppose the decrease, so product yield increases.
markingPoints: The equilibrium shifts in the exothermic forward direction to oppose the decrease, so product yield increases.

questions.question: For A(g) + B(g) ⇌ 2C(g), predict the effect of increasing pressure on the equilibrium position.
questions.modelAnswer: There is no effect on the equilibrium position because there are two moles of gas on each side of the equation.
markingPoints: There is no effect on the equilibrium position because there are two moles of gas on each side of the equation.

questions.question: For A(g) + B(g) ⇌ 2C(g), explain how increasing pressure can affect how quickly equilibrium is reached.
questions.modelAnswer: Increasing pressure increases the concentration of gases. Particles collide more often, so both forward and reverse reactions are faster and equilibrium is reached sooner.
markingPoints: Increasing pressure increases the concentration of gases. Particles collide more often, so both forward and reverse reactions are faster and equilibrium is reached sooner.
